title: 26 AI agents rewrote a backend from Django to Rust with no human merges
content:
← All posts
Pi Dash self-evolution experiment with Muse Code and Meta Muse Spark 1.3
Pi Dash coordinated 26 Muse Code agents to rewrite its own Django backend in Rust. The main port took about ten days and cost about $350 in model usage.
Introduction#
Pi Dash is an open source agent coordination platform developed by AI Republic, that automatically assigns tasks to a team of AI agents. We used the platform to refactor its own backend. This article is a short report on how that worked.
On a Pi Dash board, agents do the issues: your own Muse Code, Claude Code, Codex or Cursor through the Pi Dash daemon, or the built-in Pi Dash Agent. The rulebook, the coordinator and the review-test-merge loop in this post are ordinary Pi Dash features. You can run the same setup on your own backlog.
Pi Dash rewrote its own backend in Rust#
In late September and early October 2026, Pi Dash coordinated 26 Muse Code agents on 5 developer machines to rewrite its own backend from Python and Django to Rust. The main port took about ten days. The agents picked up issues from a Pi Dash board, wrote the code, reviewed it, tested it against the running Django server, and merged their own pull requests.
The backend started as a fork of Plane’s Django API. By September it was about 101,000 lines of application code, plus about 20,000 lines of cloud-only code. We wanted it in Rust. We also wanted to find out whether our own product could run a project this large with no person approving each step.
It could, with caveats. This post covers the rules we gave the agents, how we checked that they were right, and what still needs improving.
Why Muse Code and Muse Spark. Every agent was Muse Code running as a Pi Dash runner, with muse-spark-1.3-contribute as the model. We chose them for two reasons:
- Price and performance. A project this size means an agent run for every step of every issue, so the cost of each run matters as much as its quality.
- Stability on long runs. The work went on for days with few people involved, so the model had to stay on task across long sessions without someone stepping in.
Across the whole project, the agents sent about 166,000 requests to the model and used about 48.6 billion tokens, for a total model cost of about $350.
The short version:
- Time: about ten days for the main port, September 26 to October 5. By then about three quarters of the final Rust code and nine in ten domain-port pull requests had merged.
- Volume: about 1,740 Pi Dash issues and about 1,320 merged pull requests.
- Correctness: 5,029 contract tests run against both backends. Every HTTP contract test passes on Rust.
- Safety: no unsafe code. Every crate forbids it.
- Process: no human approval gate on any merge.
Why leave Django#
We had three reasons.
- Python cost too much to run. The Django backend was heavy and slow: on our production host it used about 1.5 GB of memory against 81 MB for Rust, and with 32 requests at once it answered a third as many per second (The numbers has the details).
- One language from the cloud to the developer’s machine. The agent daemon and the desktop app were already Rust. With the backend in Rust too, the cloud and the daemon can share the same code.
- A backend built for running agents. The backend now hands out and tracks agent work all day, which needs a language that answers fast on few resources. Django serves more requests by adding Python processes; Rust serves them from one process.
Same behavior, new code#
Planning came first. Muse Code scanned the Django codebase and wrote a plan: it measured every area of the backend, marked dead code to skip, and split the rest into 10 foundation issues and 37 domain epics. Claude Code reviewed the plan. Muse Code then created the epics and the rulebook in Pi Dash through MCP, one issue per row of the plan. From there, each epic’s first run splits it into its own sub-issues, as the loop section shows.
Every agent run starts by reading one rulebook, a Pi Dash issue called PIDASHCONV-1. Its main rules:
- Keep the behavior. Same URLs, JSON, database schema and SQL behavior. Changing behavior needs its own issue.
- Quarantine. Code goes only under rust-api/. No Python file is touched.
- Done means green. The named tests pass. No stubs, skipped tests or placeholders.
- Review assumes the code is wrong. Two independent passes against the Python before any decision.
- Report problems, don’t work around them. A rule that can’t be followed becomes a process: comment on the rulebook.
The first rule fixed behavior, not code. Django does much of its work implicitly, through base classes, serializers, permission classes and lazy querysets, so most of it has no direct Rust equivalent. For each issue, an agent worked out what the Python actually does (the rows it reads, the checks it applies, the JSON it returns, the side effects) and wrote new Rust to match. That is closer to clean-room development: the Python was the specification, not the template. Contract tests, Python suites that send real HTTP requests, then ran against both backends to check the result.
The Rust is organized by layer, not by Django app: types → db → auth → services → api, plus jobs. The lower layers were written first and then locked.
One rule changed midway. On October 26, “same JSON” stopped meaning every byte: business behavior and the API contract must still match, but library quirks no client can trigger are no longer copied.
The loop: implement, review, test, merge#
Every issue moves through the same loop on a Pi Dash board, and each step is a separate agent run with its own fresh context. The run that writes the code never reviews it.
A review or test that finds a problem sends the issue back to Implement. A pass goes straight to the merge, in the same run.
The coordinator is a scheduled Pi Dash agent that acts as project manager. It frees issues whose stage is open and whose blockers are done. It re-dispatches stuck runs, turns process: comments into issues and reports progress. It never touches code.
Epics split themselves. Each Django domain started as one epic. Its first run read the Python and filed sub-issues bottom-up: serializers, then models, queries, permissions, tasks, handlers, with at most five units each. A review run checked that split against the source before any sub-issue could start.
Merging is the test run’s job. The merge procedure has five steps:
- Merge the issues this one depends on first.
- Rebase on the Rust branch.
- Re-run the affected checks.
- Wait for the one required check.
- Squash-merge and post the commit SHA.
If other pull requests keep landing first, the run may rebase up to six times before it stops and reports.
Red CI after a merge is never reverted. GitHub runs the full Rust suite after each merge. If it goes red, the coordinator files one urgent fix issue naming the failing tests and the merges since the last green run. The fix run bisects that range using only the failing tests.
The numbers#
Most of the code was written in about ten days. From September 26 to October 5, agents merged about 720,000 net lines of Rust, about three quarters of what was there when the branch merged into main. By October 12 it was about 88%. The domain ports themselves ran from September 27 to October 10, and 353 of their 395 pull requests had merged by October 5. The weeks after went to fixes, parity work and cleanup, and to time spent waiting for us to check results and decide what came next. The branch merged into main on November 3.
After October 12 the pace dropped to a few thousand lines a day across all merges, as the work moved to fixes, parity and cleanup.
The Rust is about five times longer than the Python it replaced. Django does much of its work implicitly: the ORM writes the SQL, and DRF serializers and permission classes do the rest. Rust spells out each query, each JSON field and each check.

Both backends run on the same production host and database, so we compared them dir

report.summary: Pi Dash ran 26 AI coding agents for ten days to port its own Django backend to Rust, merging 1,320 pull requests with no human approval.
report.background: Agentic coding tools have moved from autocomplete to multi-file edits, but most teams still keep a human on every merge. Pi Dash, an open-source agent coordination platform from AI Republic, decided to test the limit on its own codebase. Its backend began as a fork of Plane's Django API and had grown to roughly 101,000 lines of application code plus 20,000 lines of cloud-only code. The team wanted Rust for three reasons: the Django service used about 1.5 GB of memory versus 81 MB for Rust, handled a third the throughput at 32 concurrent requests, and forced a split between a Rust daemon/desktop app and a Python server. The experiment also served as a product test: could Pi Dash manage a project this large with no person approving each step, using Muse Code agents on the muse-spark-1.3-contribute model?
key_points: Scale and cost were modest: about 166,000 model requests, 48.6 billion tokens and roughly $350 in model usage. That produced about 1,740 issues and 1,320 merged pull requests, with agents landing around 720,000 net lines of Rust in ten days. A scheduled coordinator agent acted as project manager, freeing blocked issues and re-dispatching stuck runs, but never touched code.

A single rulebook issue governed every run: keep identical behavior, put new code only under rust-api/, treat 'done' as named tests passing with no stubs, and assume any review will find the code wrong. Agents were told to report unfollowable rules as process issues rather than work around them. One rule was relaxed midway, so byte-identical JSON no longer had to match library quirks no client could trigger.

Every issue moved through implement, review, test and merge as separate agent runs with fresh context, so the run that wrote code never reviewed it. The test run performed the merge: rebase, re-run affected checks, wait for the required check, squash-merge and post the commit SHA. Red CI after a merge was never reverted; the coordinator instead filed an urgent fix issue that bisected the failing range.

Because Django does much of its work implicitly through ORM, serializers and permission classes, there was no direct Rust translation. Agents treated the Python as a specification rather than a template, clean-room style, and wrote roughly five times as much Rust organized by layer (types, db, auth, services, api, jobs). Lower layers were written first and then locked.

Correctness was checked with 5,029 contract tests that send real HTTP requests to both backends, and every HTTP contract test passes on Rust. No unsafe code was allowed and every crate forbids it. The authors still note caveats and areas needing improvement, and the branch took until early November to merge into main once fixes and parity work finished.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the headline is less about Rust than about process: the bottleneck in autonomous coding is verification, not generation. Rulebooks, adversarial review, contract tests and deterministic merge procedures did the work a human approver usually does. Teams will likely copy this pattern of small, single-purpose agent runs with fresh context and hard gates. For developers, it shows large migrations can be attempted with modest model budgets, but only where behavior is testable and the spec is executable. Expect more investment in contract tests, CI guardrails and coordinator agents, plus a new benchmark question: not 'can agents write code' but 'can you prove it still behaves'. For users, cheaper, smaller-footprint services and faster iteration are the upside; the risk is silent behavioral drift where no contract test exists.
report.tools: Watch Pi Dash (open-source agent coordination board with an MCP interface) and Muse Code with muse-spark-1.3-contribute as a long-run coding model; Claude Code, Codex and Cursor can plug into the same board as runners. To replicate the approach, invest in contract testing against a live reference server, strict CI checks, and Rust crates that forbid unsafe code. The Plane Django API is a useful large reference codebase if you want to try a comparable clean-room port yourself.
